sections.content:
Course Content: Signal and Systems (Prof. Miao Wenchao)

Professor Miao’s Signal and Systems course covers the following core topics in depth:

Introduction to Signals and Systems – Classification of signals (continuous-time vs. discrete-time, periodic, aperiodic, energy/power signals), basic signal operations, and system properties (linearity, time-invariance, causality, stability).

Linear Time-Invariant (LTI) Systems – Impulse response, convolution integral (continuous-time), convolution sum (discrete-time), and step-by-step evaluation of convolution with detailed examples.

Fourier Series – Trigonometric and exponential Fourier series representation of periodic signals, symmetry properties, and how the series approximates signals.

Fourier Transform – Derivation from Fourier series, Fourier transform pairs, properties (linearity, time shift, frequency shift, scaling, duality, convolution theorem, Parseval’s theorem), and spectral analysis of aperiodic signals.

Laplace Transform – Definition, region of convergence (ROC), inverse Laplace transform, and application to continuous-time system analysis (transfer functions, poles/zeros, stability).

Z-Transform – Definition, ROC, properties, and application to discrete-time system analysis, including system function and frequency response.

Sampling and Signal Reconstruction – The sampling theorem (Nyquist rate), aliasing, and reconstruction of continuous-time signals from their samples.

Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) – Basic concept of DFT as a sampled version of the DTFT, but the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm is not covered.

Important Note:
Because the FFT is not taught in this course, students who need that material — especially for computationally efficient spectral analysis or DSP applications — should take ELEC 3100 (or the equivalent course at your institution), where FFT and advanced digital signal processing topics are treated in detail.
sections.teaching:
Professor Miao is a kind and knowledgeable instructor, but I have to be honest: his voice is often too soft during lectures, so attending class in person isn’t something I’d strongly recommend for every student. The real star of this course, however, is his slide deck. His slides are absolutely outstanding — textbook quality, even reference-level. They’re the kind of materials you’ll want to save as a permanent collection. He gives the historical background of key equations, works through convolution examples step by step, and everything is presented so clearly that you won’t need to rely on AI tools (and risk hallucinations). The slides alone make this course excellent for revision and self-study.

The Instructional Assistant (IA) is equally exceptional. She teaches with real dedication and heart, has excellent intuition, and explains concepts step by step. She’s a local, so Cantonese is not an issue at all. You’ll usually find her in Room 2395. She truly embraces the philosophy of “teaching you how to fish” rather than just giving you the answer — no matter what problem you’re stuck on, she’ll guide you through it patiently. Both she and Professor Miao are extremely nice and approachable people.

That said, please don’t underestimate this course — it is non-trivial. You should budget at least two full days to properly digest each homework assignment, which is crucial preparation for both the midterm and the final exam.

sections.workload:
Please do not underestimate this course — it is non-trivial by every measure.

Overall: You should budget at least 2 full days to fully digest each homework assignment. The homework is crucial preparation for both the midterm and the final examination. In fact, one student review from a similar Signals and Systems course noted: "The homeworks, though quite tedious... but it is extremely rewarding in the end. His tests were fair, and if you did your homework, you would do well on them."

Homework: The assignments are tedious and mathematically heavy — especially the impulse train problems, which require careful handling of infinite series and sampling representations. These are not problems you can rush through in an evening.

Labs: The labs are equally non-trivial and demand significant programming effort. The core idea is to use the SciPy library (particularly scipy.signal) to generate the required diagrams that match the theoretical results from Professor Miao's slides. For impulse train generation, you can use scipy.signal.unit_impulse to create multiple impulses by specifying a list of pulse locations.
If you get stuck on generating a specific diagram, a practical workflow is:
(1) understand the theory from the slides first,
(2) write your own SciPy code,
(3) if the plot doesn't match, use an AI coding assistant to help debug your script and align the output with what the slides show.

sections.content: ELEC 2100 is a well-structured introductory course that provides a solid foundation in electrical engineering concepts. The course covers fundamental topics in a clear and progressive way, making it accessible even to students without a strong electronics background. The lectures are generally clear and supported by examples that help connect theory to practical applications. While some parts require regular practice to fully understand the concepts, the overall workload is manageable. This course is useful for gaining basic intuition in circuits and signals and is relevant for students interested in engineering applications in other fields.
sections.teaching: The teaching is clear and well structured. The instructor explains the concepts in a progressive way and uses examples to illustrate the theory. The pace is reasonable, although some topics may require personal review to fully understand. Overall, the teaching quality is satisfactory.
sections.grading: The grading scheme is transparent and consistent with the course content. Assessment is mainly based on exams and problem-solving, which fairly reflect the material covered in class. The grading is reasonable, provided that the concepts are well understood and practiced.
sections.workload: The workload is moderate and in line with the number of credits. Regular practice is needed to keep up with the course, especially before assessments, but the workload remains manageable throughout the semester.

sections.workload:
Very difficult, I need to pay a lot of time to understand the concepts... I almost learn this course for around one year.

Let me list out the difficulties between different topics.
(Full mark 10 marks, which you may need to do lots of revision and help from Professor and TAs.)

1. Complex number, complex signals and basic functions. (0/10)
Easy, if you have difficulties of first few lectures you may have serious background issues, you may really need to reconsider whether you can take this course this semester.

2. Basic properties of signal and systems. (3/10)
Quite okay la, maybe the properties is quite abstract. Sometimes the signal maybe confusing and asking you whether the signal is memoryless/causal/stable/LTI.
Maybe you need to have a good understanding about those basic properties and pay attention to examples in lecture notes.

3. Impulse response and convolution. (6/10)
The story starts to be interesting and difficult. The meaning of impulse response and convolution are abstract.
But the operation of convolution and polynomial multiplication are exactly the same, we can use z-transform to prove that.
(x^2+2x+1)(x+1)
(delta[n-2] + 2*delta[n-1] + delta[n]) * (delta[n-1] + delta[n])
They are exactly same in operation.

4. Fourier series and transforms. (8/10)
This part is going to be middle boss. The main idea is not that hard: we would like to know how much amount of signal under the specific frequency. The first principal is easy but many abstract mathematical properties with proofs.

5. Sampling theorem and aliasing. (9/10)
This part is very difficult, the prove of sampling theorem in frequency domain is very hard to understand. Maybe first from time domain to prove sampling theorem as a good approach.

6. Spectrum analysis, FFT, OFDM. (10/10)
Monster, this is the most difficult lecture in this course. I even cannot understand what 9 it is after getting A+...

7. Differential equations and Laplace transform. (8/10)
If you take MATH2351 or Laplace transform in previous, the difficulty can be reduced to between 5-7. This is generalization of FT and some properties are more or less similar.

Given Isabel’s teaching pace can be describe in an idiom, 一言既出，駟馬難追. Not means she is trustworthy, is even four horses cannot chase her pace🫠. It totally ruins the learning experience given the concepts are extremely abstract and not understandable. If you can just understand all the concepts and do the homework sets. You will have absolute advantage in the exam. Even you have many careless I think you still can get A or above.

Ask questions IMMEDIATELY after lectures if you get confused and lost. MY always be here with you. At lease you don’t like a prince and princess who always escaping or not focusing on both lectures and tutorials and just waiting for “answers” and additional tutorials. This is a difficult course. Good Luck!

sections.content:
从名字就可以看出来，内容是信号与系统。一个信号，咱甭管是啥玩意。经过一个系统的处理之后得到了输出的结果。这门课从头到尾都是在干这一件事情。

从最基础的复数运算讲起，然后讲到一些常见的信号函数，西格玛(t)：impulse u(t) 方波函数这些。将信号的类型分为连续时间CT和离散时间DT的。这一段的难点就是要熟悉complex sinusoid（e^st e^jwt ) 的表示形式和运算方法。完后是系统的性质，小难，需要通过系统输入输出或者说响应函数来判断系统的性质。讲他的主要目的就是引入重要的LTI——线性时不变系统。紧接着是第一个大头内容———卷积（convolution）。听着是不是头就大了。LTI处理信号的方式就是卷积。这个货得理解好半天，自己计算操作的时候我觉得你就按着notes里面给的步骤一步一步来就行。

前面唠了一大顿，正主才刚来。这就是激动人心的傅里叶分析。他会放慢脚步详细地介绍离散时间和连续时间下的傅里叶级数和傅里叶变换。傅里叶级数用于把周期函数进行正交分解，分解为多个弦函数相加的形式。这样更好处理。而傅里叶变换则是将信号从时间领域转换到频率领域来分析他的特征。这样可以把在时间领域难以进行卷积计算的信号与系统放到频率领域进行简单的计算处理。概括很精炼但是要你一个月时间来学习吃透他。

后面就会轻松一点，讲了一些傅里叶分析的简单应用，如AM FM通信，取样的原理，用DT办法处理CT信号。以及频谱分析仪，DFT，FFT的方法。QAM，OFDM这些当代传输字符串的方法。给ELEC3100开门。考试可能在这里抠细节，一定要把犄角旮旯都整明白。

最后几节课将会速通拉普拉斯变换，介绍一下收敛范围ROC（别想到海的那边去了）ROC与系统性质的关系。简单介绍拉普拉斯在控制系统中应用的小案例，给ELEC3200开门。这段最好还是理解一下，但是后面不上这俩课的话背下来就可以。没什么所谓。

总而言之呢，这门课就是算明白数为王，不用太理解，作业反复做给他提了明白扒拉干净。看到那道题一下就能想起来怎么做就OK。

sections.content:
ELEC2100 is about learning a set of languages (mathematics, English, and Matlab) and the practice of the use of a fundamental set of mathematical relationships to model engineering problems related to signal processing, communication, and control.

Topics include CT and DT signals, impulse and frequency response, CT/DT Fourier Series/Transform, sampling theorem, differential equation representation of system and Laplace Transform.

ELEC2100 requires understanding and you do not need to memorize anything as important math relations will all be provided in the exams.
sections.teaching:
All materials are released week by week.
2 lectures(ppt. with video) are included every week.
You need to study the material before going to classmeet.

-In Class(before midterm)-
1.Review of key video lecture concepts by instructor (20 mins)
2.Group-based exercise (20 mins). Students form groups of 4 to work on a small number of sample problems.
3.Review of example problems by instructor (10 mins).
4.Individual exercise(20 mins)

But in this semester, after the midterm, some students complain that the workload each week is too heavy and changes were made:
-In Class(after midterm)-
1.Group-based exercise (~30-40 mins)..
2.Review of key video lecture concepts while reviewing example problems by instructor (~30-40 mins).
3.You can take the individual exercise back home to finish it and submit it at the beginning of next classmeet.

MY is a really good tutor. Even if you do not study the online material, you can still get a good result if you go to the tutorial every week.

sections.teaching: When I take this course, they have changed to so-call "Blended Learning", which all the lectures are online. The "lecture" you see on the timetable is actually a class meet which you are provided with exercises to do it there, and those are graded. The online lectures are a bit boring, but it will be difficult for you to understand the topics just by reading the powerpoint, luckily the video can be sped up so it souldn't be a big problem. The TA hosting the tutorials explain the topics pretty well. Even if you are so busy that you didn't watch the lecture video, you are still strongly recommended to attend the tutorials.

sections.content: The content had a lot of mathematics in it. Complex numbers, Fourier and Laplace analysis were the primary topics of the course.

The TA MY Chang, on the other hand, was great. Her tutorials were very important and I would suggest you attend them, for great revision.
